Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

issues.item: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Hard to Recall Deliberately' conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' Deliberate retrieval difficulty and very easy verbal access are opposing states and are hard to reconcile as describing the same patient at the same time, especially alongside 'Overwhelm on Recall,' which implies traumatic recall is effortful and dysregulating rather than easy to discuss.

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' directly conflicts with 'When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop.' At this severity level and with strong Trigger↔Memory and Memory→Threat links, these two memory items describe opposing levels of accessibility/distress and are hard to reconcile as the same current presentation.

issues.item: Triggers: Authority Commands: Being given orders or instructions
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile with stalking as the index trauma: 'authority commands' and especially 'bicycle' do not show an evident clinical link to the reported trauma, and the profile provides no memory or appraisal content that would make these idiosyncratic triggers understandable.

Threat items emphasize broad interpersonal attack and generic danger vigilance (loud sounds, scanning exits, watching others for harm), which fits assault/combat/fire trauma better than stalking. For stalking, one would expect threat focused more on being followed, approached, monitored, contacted, or found by the perpetrator.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'I am a weak person' sits awkwardly with this profile and occupation unless supported by appraisal content about failure to protect oneself or family; here the other appraisals center on permanent damage and fear of going crazy, so the weakness item feels less coherent with the stalking-specific formulation than those items.

vignette:
Nabil is a 37-year-old firefighter who came to treatment months after a stalking ordeal that had ended on paper but not in his body. He described the beginning of it in fragments rather than a smooth story. A man he had encountered repeatedly around the station and later near his home began appearing in places that should not have overlapped: outside the grocery store, across from the school where his wife worked, beside intersections on a bicycle, waiting just long enough for Nabil to notice him. At first he told himself it was coincidence. What changed things was the growing pattern of being behind him—on foot, in a car mirror, or most vividly, the cyclist trailing him at a measured distance as he drove home after shift. By the time police became involved, Nabil had started taking longer routes and circling blocks to check whether he was being tracked. He remembers the sick certainty of looking up and seeing that bicycle again, close enough to feel deliberate.

Since then, physical locations have become loaded in ways that make immediate sense to him. Pulling into the station parking lot, stopping near the intersection where he used to spot the cyclist, or even entering public buildings with long sightlines can bring the whole memory back without warning. In those moments, the place seems to tell Nabil something condemning about himself: that a normal man would not be thrown by a parking lot or a glimpse of open space, and that the fact he is means he has been changed into someone weak and unreliable. He does not experience it as ordinary remembering. It arrives all at once, with a rush of emotion so strong that he has to cut himself off and focus on something concrete in front of him. After one of these episodes, the thought that follows is often immediate and brutal: if a memory can still take him over like this, then something in him must be seriously wrong and perhaps permanently so. When asked to describe exactly what happened over those months, he often says he knows it clearly but cannot find words for it; after a sentence or two, he goes quiet, jaw tight, as if continuing would flood him.

Those moments have changed what he believes about himself. Each time a place or the sense of someone behind him pulls the memory up so forcefully, Nabil thinks, this is not how a solid man reacts. He has come to believe he has permanently changed for the worse since the stalking, and that the intensity of his reactions means he may be going crazy. More than once he said the part he cannot forgive is feeling frightened by something other people might dismiss, which to him proves he is weak. When he is caught in that self-accusation, the stalking scenes come back more easily and with sharper force, as if his mind keeps returning to them to confirm the verdict he has already reached about himself. That conclusion has made the triggers feel even more potent: a hallway, a parking lot, the glimpse of a bicycle is no longer just a reminder of what happened, but evidence, in his mind, of what he has become. Once he has decided that he is damaged and unable to trust his own reactions, ordinary details catch and hold in a way they never used to; a cyclist at a distance or footsteps behind him register immediately as meaningful, as if his own weakness has trained him to spot danger everywhere.

At work, this has narrowed his world in ways that embarrass him. As soon as he enters any building, even ones he has been in many times on calls, he scans for exits automatically. Unexpected loud sounds keep him on high alert beyond what he considers normal for the job, and he watches people closely for signs they might harm him, especially anyone lingering near doors or hanging back behind the group. He knows firefighting requires vigilance, but he feels his vigilance has become personal and relentless. Living in that constant state of readiness has become, for Nabil, its own proof that he is no longer the steady person he was before; the fact that he cannot stand down from danger feels to him like evidence that the stalking has permanently altered him. Because he believes something in him has broken, he treats every jolt in his body as proof that he cannot trust himself to settle. That belief keeps him keyed up, and the more he remains keyed up, the more convinced he becomes that he is damaged.

The memories and his watchfulness feed each other. When something in the environment abruptly brings back the image of being followed, his body shifts into immediate surveillance: where are the exits, who is near me, who is watching me, what was that sound? Once in that state, every movement around him feels potentially significant. The intrusive image seems to prime the world itself; after it hits, even routine sounds and passing figures stand out as possible signs, and he moves through the next minutes as if the memory has taught him what to notice. On bad days at the station, if he hears a sudden clang and then notices someone outside near the apparatus bay, his mind leaps back to the stalking before he can slow it down. Later he berates himself for reacting so strongly, telling himself that a stronger man would have shaken this off long ago. Those judgments do not calm him; they make the next memory harder to bear, and they leave him even more convinced that the next place, the next bicycle, the next sensation of someone behind him will undo him again.

Over time he has also begun to enter spaces already braced for the old pattern. If he has to walk from the station lot or cross a downtown block after a call, he is half-expecting to feel tracked, and that expectancy makes ordinary locations feel contaminated before anything has happened. When he does catch sight of a cyclist or senses footsteps behind him, the memory snaps into place so quickly that he feels ambushed by his own surroundings. His wife has noticed that he chooses seats with a view of the door, studies strangers in restaurants, and occasionally cuts outings short without explaining why. At home, he has tried to explain the stalking to her, but when he reaches the parts that matter most, he loses the words and shuts down, which leaves him ashamed and more certain that something fundamental in him has given way.

He sought help after realizing that the problem was beginning to affect his work and marriage in ways he could no longer hide behind discipline. He recently left a family gathering abruptly after hearing a loud noise outside and becoming convinced, for several minutes, that someone was there watching the house. What frightened him most was not only the fear itself but the thought that this might be permanent—that he will keep living as if pursuit is always about to resume, and that his wife will come to know him only as this guarded, scanning version of himself. What he hopes for, cautiously, is not to forget what happened but to walk into a room, hear a sound, or see a bicycle without feeling his whole mind and body seized by it.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly show triggers directly leading to negative appraisals within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not clearly show negative appraisals directly bringing on intrusive memory within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly show negative appraisals directly making triggers more likely or more salient within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly show traumatic memory directly causing negative appraisals within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly show traumatic memory directly making triggers more likely or more salient within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly show threat or hypervigilance directly leading to negative appraisals within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
